entries.topic: Ancestry and language: what the genome studies show for each Jewish community

claims.text: The study genotyped 121 people from 14 Jewish communities, among them Ashkenazi, Sephardi (Turkey, Bulgaria), Moroccan, Georgian, Azerbaijani, Iranian, Iraqi, Uzbekistani (Bukharan), Bene Israel (Mumbai), Cochini (Kerala), Ethiopian (Beta Israel) and Yemenite Jews.
Most Jewish samples form a tight cluster overlying Druze and Cypriot samples; the authors trace the origins of most Jewish diaspora communities to the Levant.

Within that cluster, one subgroup is Ashkenazi, Moroccan and Sephardi Jews; another is the Middle Eastern (Iranian, Iraqi) and Caucasus (Azerbaijani, Georgian) Jewish communities. Yemenite Jews form a separate compact cluster that overlaps mainly with Bedouin and also with Saudi samples.
The European-associated ancestry component is more substantial in Ashkenazi, Moroccan and Sephardi Jews than in the Middle Eastern Jewish communities. The paper gives no admixture percentages.

Ethiopian Jews (Beta Israel) and Indian Jews (Bene Israel and Cochini) cluster with neighbouring local populations in Ethiopia and western India, despite a clear paternal link between the Bene Israel and the Levant.
Ethiopian Jews clustered with Semitic-speaking rather than Cushitic-speaking Ethiopians.

A 2016 genome study of the Bene Israel found substantial Jewish and substantial Indian ancestry, mixed within the last thousand years (about 19–33 generations ago) and involving Middle Eastern Jews, with more Jewish ancestry on the male side and more local ancestry on the female side.
